_what_this_is: Negative control: concurrent call pairs that share LANGUAGE STRUCTURE and NO INFORMATION. Every match the matcher claims between two calls of one family is a false positive, because neither call's arguments caused the other's request. See docs/CALIBRATION.md.

families.api: a search endpoint: JSON {query} in, GET /api/search?q=<plus-encoded> out

arguments.query: how to rotate a database password
how to compress a video file
how to list open pull requests
how to configure a reverse proxy
how to export a spreadsheet as csv
how to restore a deleted branch

families.shared_structure_note: the JSON envelope, the path prefix, the opening phrase, and plus-encoding of every space
families.why: Free-text search is the most common shape an agent sends and the one where shared English carries the most bytes. Every call here begins with the same four words, which is not a trick: an agent asking a documentation search engine phrases its questions the same way every time.

families.api: a REST read: JSON {owner, repo, path} in, GET /repos/<owner>/<repo>/contents/<path> out
families.shared_structure_note: the JSON keys, both path prefixes, the docs/ directory, the .md extension and kebab-case naming throughout
families.why: Structured arguments reassembled into a path. Included precisely because it is expected to behave BETTER than free text: the JSON envelope never reaches the wire, so the only shared runs are path segments. A negative corpus of only the hard shapes would overstate the rate.

families.api: a fetch: JSON {url} in, GET <path of that url> out, same host throughout
families.shared_structure_note: one host, one /guides/ prefix, a section segment shared by groups of calls, and kebab-case leaf names
families.why: Sibling documents on one site. The section prefix is shared because that is what a site taxonomy is, and several leaves start with the same letters, which is what sibling pages look like. This family is where the rate should depend on k most sharply, since the shared run is the prefix plus however many leaf characters happen to agree.

families.shared_structure_note: the JSON keys, the locale enum, the wrapper keys the server adds, and ordinary English sentences
families.why: The worst case, and the most ordinary one. Every call carries the same locale enum and the same key names, and the server's body repeats them verbatim, so a 16-byte run of shared field structure exists in every pair before a single word of the payload is compared. This is the family that makes the case for weighting a k-gram by how common it is.

families.api: a repository contents API: JSON {owner, repo, path?, ref?} in, GET /repos/<owner>/<repo>/... out
families.shared_structure_note: the JSON envelope, the /repos/ prefix, two organisations and two repository names shared across the family, and a path vocabulary drawn from one repository layout
families.why: The other four families in this corpus were authored against a k-gram matcher and share long literal runs. Structural containment does not read runs at all, so those families cannot falsify it and a rate of zero over them means only that they were built for a different instrument. This family is built against containment itself: a call whose tokens are a proper subset of another call's request, two calls sharing an enum value and nothing else, and one repository reached through two organisations. Five of its eight calls carry no information of their own and say so in an explicit information_free field, because a call that owns no distinguishing value is precisely the call containment gets wrong, and it cannot be built with one.

calls.why: The full call, and the request every subset case below is measured against.
Its two tokens are a proper subset of call 01's request tokens, so containment claims it caused call 01's request. It did not. The family's headline case.
calls.information_free: Carries no value of its own. That is the attack and not an omission: containment asks whether every token of a call is present in a request, so a call that owns nothing unique is contained in any request that mentions its organisation and repository. A call with a distinguishing value could not be a subset of another call's request, so this case cannot be built any other way.

calls.why: A second subset one token longer, so the attack is visibly a property of containment and not of any particular minimum token count.

pair_rule: ordered pairs WITHIN a family only: (A, B) asks whether a k-gram of B's arguments appears in A's request. Cross-family pairs share no structure, so counting them would deflate the rate with cases nobody finds hard.
